analysis.investment_thesis: Bai-Kakaji Polymers fails both Magic Formula criteria decisively — earnings yield of ~4.9% (P/E 20.3) is well below the 6% minimum, and ROE of 0.41% signals ROIC is abysmal, nowhere near the 20%+ threshold. This is neither cheap nor good; it is the exact opposite of a Magic Formula candidate.
key_strengths: Debt profile not flagged as distressed
key_risks: ROE of 0.41% implies near-zero return on capital — business is not 'good'
Commodity plastics industry with weak pricing power and low moat
red_flags: ROE 0.41% — essentially not earning its cost of capital
P/E 20.3 on such low profitability is unjustifiable
Small-cap (INR 372 Cr) plastics trader/manufacturer — limited scale economics
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks on two axes: Earnings Yield (EBIT/EV) and Return on Capital. Bai-Kakaji fails both. An inverted P/E of 20.3 gives an earnings yield near 4.9% — below my 6% floor and nowhere near the 12%+ I look for. ROE at 0.41% is the more damning number: even if leverage inflates or deflates this vs. ROIC, a business earning under 1% on equity is not generating economic profit. This is the opposite of "a good business at a bargain price" — it is a mediocre business at a full price.

The systematic screen would never let this into a portfolio. Plastic products is a fragmented, low-margin, capital-intensive industry where only scale players earn decent returns on capital, and a INR 372 Cr company trading at 20x earnings with sub-1% ROE has neither scale nor quality nor valuation support. I'd exclude it on quantitative grounds without needing to read further.
